# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium. Once considered a rare and untreatable condition, CA is now increasingly recognized as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), aortic stenosis, and conduction disease [1,2]. The two predominant types affecting the heart are immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis, the latter subdivided into wild-type (ATTRwt) and hereditary (ATTRv) forms [3]. Advances in noninvasive imaging and the emergence of disease-modifying therapies have transformed the diagnostic and therapeutic landscape over the past decade [4,5].

## Epidemiology and Pathophysiology

AL amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia producing amyloidogenic light chains, with an estimated incidence of approximately 10 cases per million person-years [6]. ATTRwt predominantly affects elderly men and is now recognized in up to 13% of patients hospitalized with HFpEF and in a substantial proportion of patients with severe aortic stenosis [7,8]. ATTRv results from pathogenic variants in the *TTR* gene; the Val122Ile variant is notably prevalent among individuals of West African ancestry [9].

The pathophysiology differs by type. In AL disease, circulating light chains exert direct proteotoxic effects on cardiomyocytes in addition to fibril deposition, contributing to the rapid clinical deterioration characteristic of this form [10]. In ATTR disease, destabilization of the transthyretin tetramer leads to monomer misfolding and fibril aggregation, producing progressive ventricular wall thickening and diastolic dysfunction [11].

## Clinical Presentation

CA should be suspected in patients with unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, HFpEF in older adults, low-voltage ECG disproportionate to wall thickness, and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome [12]. Extracardiac clues include lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, and autonomic dysfunction [13]. AL amyloidosis may additionally present with nephrotic-range proteinuria, periorbital purpura, and macroglossia [14]. Conduction system involvement and atrial arrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation, are common, and intracardiac thrombus may occur even in sinus rhythm [15].

## Diagnosis

Echocardiography typically reveals increased wall thickness, biatrial enlargement, and a characteristic "apical sparing" pattern of longitudinal strain [16]. Cardiac magnetic resonance demonstrates diffuse late gadolinium enhancement and elevated extracellular volume, supporting the diagnosis [17]. A major advance has been the validation of bone scintigraphy using technetium-labeled tracers (e.g., ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pyrophosphate or DPD), which can establish a diagnosis of ATTR-CA noninvasively when monoclonal protein is excluded by serum and urine immunofixation and free light-chain assay [18,19]. Grade 2–3 myocardial uptake in the absence of a monoclonal gammopathy has a specificity approaching 100% for ATTR-CA [19]. Endomyocardial biopsy with Congo red staining and mass spectrometry–based typing remains the gold standard when noninvasive findings are equivocal or AL disease is suspected [20]. Accurate typing is essential because management differs fundamentally between subtypes [21].

## Management

Treatment of AL-CA centers on plasma-cell–directed chemotherapy. The addition of the anti-CD38 antibody daratumumab to bortezomib-based regimens has improved hematologic and cardiac responses [22]. Autologous stem cell transplantation benefits selected low-risk patients [23]. Prognosis in AL disease is strongly determined by cardiac biomarkers, and staging systems incorporating troponin and natriuretic peptides guide risk stratification [24].

For ATTR-CA, the TTR stabilizer tafamidis reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in the landmark ATTR-ACT trial and remains a cornerstone of therapy [25]. Gene-silencing agents, including the small interfering RNA patisiran and the antisense oligonucleotide inotersen, were initially approved for hereditary polyneuropathy, and newer agents continue to be evaluated for the cardiac phenotype [26,27]. Acoramidis, another stabilizer, demonstrated clinical benefit in a recent randomized trial [28]. Emerging approaches include CRISPR-based in vivo gene editing targeting *TTR*, which has shown durable reductions in circulating transthyretin [29].

Supportive heart failure management requires caution: loop diuretics are central, whereas many neurohormonal agents and calcium channel blockers are poorly tolerated owing to the restrictive physiology and risk of hypotension [30]. Anticoagulation is generally recommended for atrial fibrillation given the elevated thromboembolic risk [15].

## Conclusion

Cardiac amyloidosis has evolved from an orphan disease into a treatable cause of heart failure. Heightened clinical suspicion, judicious use of noninvasive imaging, and accurate subtyping enable earlier diagnosis, while an expanding therapeutic armamentarium—including TTR stabilizers, gene silencers, and gene editing—offers genuine hope for improved outcomes. Future priorities include refining screening strategies, validating therapies specifically in the cardiac phenotype, and ensuring equitable access to costly disease-modifying treatments.
